scenes.heading: Hook · 0:00–0:44
scenes.text: Ever wondered how you could tell what is in a clear liquid, when it looks exactly like water? Here are four test tubes. One is water. One has sugar dissolved in it, one protein, one starch. They are all colourless, and nothing your eyes can do will tell them apart. Yet in a practical exam you will be handed tubes like these and asked to say, with evidence, what is in each. You do it by giving each tube the conditions under which one class of substance shows itself.

scenes.heading: Why this one is on you · 0:44–1:20
scenes.text: This is a section where the syllabus says describe and carry out. Paper 3 can require you to carry out and interpret these tests: labelled bottles, a water bath, unknown solutions, your own hands. So you need to know every object on that bench, what each reagent is for and, above all, why each step is done the way it is, because that is what lets you read a result that went wrong.

scenes.heading: What you will be able to do · 1:20–2:01
scenes.text: By the end of this you will be able to describe and carry out the Benedict's test for reducing sugars, the iodine test for starch, the emulsion test for lipids and the biuret test for proteins. You will be able to record what you observe in a proper table and infer what each result means, and what it does not mean. And you will be able to look at a doubtful result and check its conditions and controls before you conclude anything.

scenes.heading: THE ONE IDEA · conditions, observation, inference · 2:01–2:57
scenes.text: Before any apparatus, one idea, and if you hold it the rest stops being a list. Every one of these tests makes something in the sample show itself. You give the tube the conditions that one class of substance needs to produce a visible result: for reducing sugars, copper ions in excess and heat; for starch, iodine; for lipids, ethanol and then water; for proteins, alkali and copper. Then you record what you see, a colour or a cloudiness, and only then do you say what class it points to. Conditions, observation, inference, always in that order, and always with a control beside it so you know what "unchanged" looks like.

scenes.heading: The bench: name everything before you touch anything · 2:57–3:51
scenes.text: Start at the rack in front of you. Label each tube before you use it, so its result can be traced to the sample. Beside it is the syringe or measuring cylinder for measuring volumes. Give each reagent its own dropper pipette to prevent contamination. The water bath is at the back right, with a thermometer; use the holder when moving hot tubes. Read colours against the white tile at the front left. Put your eye protection on before opening a bottle. The labelled reagents wait at the back left; distilled water is there for rinsing and controls. You will meet each reagent as its test begins.

scenes.heading: Benedict's, part one: measured sample, reagent in excess · 3:51–4:53
scenes.text: Start with Benedict's. Eye protection on, because this reagent is an irritant. Label a tube, then measure two cubic centimetres of the sample into it with the syringe. Now the reagent, and here is the first rule with a reason. Use Benedict's solution in excess. Benedict's contains copper(II) ions, and they are what react with a reducing sugar; if the reagent runs out before the sugar does, the colour tells you about the reagent, not the sample. Here we illustrate two cubic centimetres of sample and two of Benedict's. Equal volumes alone do not establish chemical excess: that depends on the concentrations. Follow the supplied practical's amounts; this mark scheme credits an equal or greater volume of Benedict's than sample. Shake gently to mix.

scenes.heading: Benedict's, part two: heat in a water bath · 4:53–5:43
scenes.text: Now heat, because the reaction between copper(II) ions and a reducing sugar needs it. Put the tube in the water bath at eighty degrees or above; the cited practical uses a boiling water bath. Not a Bunsen flame straight on the tube: a flame heats one spot, the liquid can spit out, and you cannot say what temperature it reached. For this demonstration we heat for four minutes, the time a June 2022 question used; in an exam, follow the supplied method. Lift the tube out with the holder, because it is hot, and hold it against the white tile.

scenes.heading: Benedict's, part three: reading the result · 5:43–6:42
scenes.text: Here is what you may see, and the names matter. Blue is the reagent, and a tube still blue after the specified heating is negative under these conditions. After the specified heating a positive result may appear green, yellow, orange or brick-red, with a precipitate, a solid that first clouds the liquid and then settles. It need not show every colour in sequence; these are separate endpoint tubes. Say the colour you saw and say precipitate if there was one. Green and yellow are positive results; with standards heated alike, more reducing sugar gives a colour further along that row, which is the next lesson. And red is one end of the row, not the only positive answer.

scenes.heading: Controls, and what a positive Benedict's does not tell you · 6:42–7:38
scenes.text: Two more tubes go through the same heating, every time. One with distilled water instead of the sample: it should stay blue, and if it does not, check the tube, the pipette and the reagent before trusting anything. One with a solution you know contains a reducing sugar, such as glucose: it should change, and if it does not, check the control solution, the volumes, the mixing and the heating. Those are your negative and positive controls. Now what the result means. Blue to orange tells you a reducing sugar was detected. It does not tell you which one; glucose, fructose and maltose all give it. So write "reducing sugar", not "glucose".

scenes.heading: Iodine for starch · 7:38–8:29
scenes.text: The iodine test is the quick one, and it needs no heat. Put a little of the sample on a white tile or in a tube, and add a few drops of iodine in potassium iodide solution. The solution itself is orange-brown. If starch is present it turns blue-black, and you write both words, because that is the observation the mark scheme wants. If it stays orange-brown, negative under these conditions; do a water control alongside so you know what unchanged looks like. And keep the iodine pipette for iodine only, because cross-contamination can change the colour and make the result unreliable.

scenes.heading: Emulsion test, part one: ethanol first · 8:29–9:27
scenes.text: Lipids are made visible a different way. The emulsion test uses cloudiness rather than a colour reaction, and it rests on solubility: the triglycerides in this example dissolve much more readily in ethanol than in water. Before the ethanol bottle opens, extinguish the Bunsen and keep the ethanol away from any ignition source, because ethanol is flammable; an electric water bath makes this bench easier. Then put a small amount of the sample in a dry tube, add the amount of ethanol your method specifies, about two cubic centimetres here, stopper it and shake well to extract the lipid. If solid particles remain, let them settle, so that what you pour next is the clear ethanolic extract.

scenes.heading: Emulsion test, part two: into water · 9:27–10:28
scenes.text: Now pour that clear extract into a tube of water, about the same volume, and shake again. The ethanol mixes into the water, but lipid that was dissolved in the ethanol comes out of solution as tiny droplets, and the tube goes cloudy white. That cloudy white emulsion is a positive result. A clear tube is negative under these conditions. Run a blank of ethanol and water alongside, so that any slight haze in the reagents is not mistaken for an emulsion. Water first can prevent effective extraction, so it is not the prescribed method: the exam has asked for the order, and the credited one is ethanol to the sample and shake, then into water and shake again, cloudy means lipid.

scenes.heading: Biuret test, part one: the reagents and their order · 10:28–11:28
scenes.text: Now protein. The biuret test may come as a single bottle of biuret reagent, in which case follow the supplied protocol, or, as in the June 2021 practical, as two bottles: five percent potassium hydroxide and zero point one five percent copper sulfate. With two, the order is alkali first. Measure one cubic centimetre of the sample, add one cubic centimetre of the potassium hydroxide, which is an irritant, so eye protection stays on, and shake gently, then add one cubic centimetre of the copper sulfate and shake gently again. The violet colour only develops in alkaline conditions, which is why the alkali goes in first. No heating. Leave it at least a minute for the colour to develop.

scenes.heading: Biuret test, part two: reading violet, and what it detects · 11:28–12:19
scenes.text: Hold it against the white tile. The reagent is blue. If protein is present the blue turns to a lilac, purple or violet colour; the mark scheme accepts any of those words. If it stays blue, that is negative under these conditions: the reagent's own blue, not no colour. Run a known protein and a water tube beside it as your controls. What is it detecting? The biuret test detects peptide bonds in proteins and sufficiently long peptides, at least two peptide bonds. Free amino acids give no violet colour: the reagent remains blue. So write "protein present", not "amino acids present".

scenes.heading: Recording: the table, observation before inference · 12:19–13:28
scenes.text: Every one of those results goes into a table, and the table is marked. Across the top: the sample, which test was done, what you observed, and only then what it supports. Under observation you write what you saw, in words, for every test you actually did on every tube: the colour, and a precipitate or an emulsion if there was one, including tubes that stayed blue, because a negative is a result. A test you did not do is written "not tested", not "negative". In June 2021 each solution contained one or none of the three classes, so candidates tested for protein first and stopped testing a tube once it was identified: four protein results, three reducing sugar results, two starch results. And "none" there meant none of the three tested classes detected in that supplied sample.

scenes.heading: A mixture: several tests on one sample, from fresh portions · 13:28–14:18
scenes.text: Real samples can be mixtures, and the practical papers give you one. Solution U in June 2021 was tested for protein, reducing sugar and starch from separate fresh portions, and it gave violet, blue, and blue-black. Read that as three observations: protein detected, no reducing sugar detected under these conditions, starch detected. So U contains protein and starch, the credited answer. For each test, use a fresh portion in a clean tube, just as in the staged tests. For a mixture, the difference is that you carry out all the relevant tests rather than stop when one class is detected.

scenes.heading: COMMON MISTAKE E01 · claiming more certainty than a colour match supports · 14:18–15:36
scenes.text: The June 2023 report highlighted how difficult colour matching can be, in a biuret practical where candidates made a set of known protein concentrations and compared an unknown against them. Here is an illustrative answer that claims more certainty than those results support. Read it. Look at the word "exactly". These two standards received the same colour description, purple, and the unknown matched them. So the colour alone does not justify that precision. A point estimate must be labelled approximate and supported by your comparisons. The examiners' words: the significant source of error was the difficulty of identifying the colour, and the improvement was a colorimeter, which reduces the subjectivity without removing every uncertainty. Written properly: U matches the purple standards at one point two five and two point five percent, giving an approximate estimate in that region; more closely spaced standards would refine it.

scenes.heading: Competence moment: checks before conclusions · 15:36–16:46
scenes.text: Now the part that makes you the person who knows what they are doing. A result looks wrong; what do you check before you conclude anything? If the positive control stays blue, check the control solution, the labels, the reagent volumes, the mixing and the heating before interpreting the unknown. A Benedict's tube that went green may simply hold a little reducing sugar; check the heating time, the volumes and the controls before reading anything into the shade. With a known protein that stayed blue, check that the alkali went in, that the correct amount of copper reagent was added and that the colour-development time was allowed. A clear emulsion tube can be a valid negative; check the extraction and the blank before accepting it. Controls help you distinguish a valid negative from a test that has not worked.

scenes.heading: What I told you, in place · 16:46–17:42
scenes.text: So, on the bench you now know. Each test gave the sample the conditions one class needs to show itself, and you recorded what you saw before you said what it meant. Copper ions in excess and heat, and a reducing sugar showed as a colour from green to brick-red with a precipitate. Iodine, and starch showed blue-black. Ethanol then water, and lipid showed as a cloudy emulsion. Alkali then copper, and peptide bonds showed violet. Observation first, in words, for every tube, with the test named; inference second, as a class; and a control beside every test, so you can tell a valid negative from a test that has not worked.
